title: Sharps Safety and Bloodborne Pathogens

unit.title: Clinical Office Practice and Patient Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Apply sharps safety principles, including safe handling, point-of-use disposal, and the correct use of sharps containers.
- Describe the bloodborne pathogens of concern (HBV, HCV, and HIV), their routes of transmission, and the fluids treated as potentially infectious.
- Prevent needlestick and sharps injuries using engineering controls, work-practice controls, and personal protective equipment.
- Respond correctly to a sharps or blood/body-fluid exposure by providing first aid, reporting promptly, and supporting post-exposure follow-up.
- Recognize the assistant's supervised, policy-following role and escalate unsafe conditions, exposures, and out-of-scope requests to licensed staff.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

The Bloodborne Pathogens Standard is like a rulebook that protects workers from germs that travel in blood — mainly three viruses called HBV, HCV, and HIV.

### Question 2

A sharps injury is a poke or cut from something sharp like a needle — the same way a thumbtack can poke your finger, but with the added worry of germs in blood.

### Question 3

Sharps are things that can poke or cut you, like a needle or a piece of broken glass — so we put them in a special strong box instead of the regular trash.

### Question 4

The sharps box is like a heavy, strong mailbox for used needles — once a needle goes in, it cannot poke back out and hurt anyone.

### Question 5

OPIM is a short name for body liquids that are not blood but can still carry germs — like fluid around the brain or fluid with blood in it.

### Question 6

Standard precautions are like wearing a seatbelt on every car ride — you do the safe thing every single time, not just when you think a crash might happen.

### Question 7

HBV is the one germ of the three that has a vaccine — like getting a shield before going into a game, so your body is ready to fight it off.

### Question 8

Most workplace pokes that spread blood germs come from needles — so the biggest rule is to handle needles safely and put them away right after use.

### Question 9

If you get poked, you wash the spot with soap and water right away — like cleaning a scrape — and then tell the person in charge so a doctor or nurse can help.

### Question 10

A used needle goes straight into the strong sharps box right away — the same way you put a used tissue in the bin immediately instead of setting it down.

### Question 11

Recapping with two hands is like trying to put a lid on a pen while your other hand is right in front of the point — it is easy to poke yourself.

### Question 12

The biohazard sign on the sharps box is like a warning sticker that says 'careful — sharp and germy inside!' so everyone knows to be careful.

### Question 13

Washing your hands is like cleaning the table before and after you set out a picnic — you clean before gloves go on and again after they come off.

### Question 14

Gloves are like an apron when you paint — they help keep you clean, but they can still tear, so you still need to be careful and wash up.

### Question 15

An engineering control is a gadget that protects you automatically, like a needle that tucks its own sharp point away so it cannot poke you.

### Question 16

A work-practice control is a smart habit, like always putting the needle away right where you used it so you never carry it around.

### Question 17

If your job might put you near blood, the boss has to offer you the hepatitis B shot for free — like the company providing safety gear for the job.

### Question 18

The exposure control plan is like a fire-safety plan for blood germs — it writes down who might be at risk and exactly what steps keep everyone safe.

### Question 19

Blood germs get in through openings — a poke, a cut, or getting a splash in your eye, nose, or mouth — not by just standing nearby.

### Question 20

You should never reach your hand into the sharps box — that is like sticking your hand into a box of thumbtacks on purpose.

### Question 21

You should never bend, snap, or re-cap a used needle with your fingers — the less you fiddle with it, the less chance it pokes you.

### Question 22

Handing a needle to someone is like passing an open pair of scissors point-first — too easy for one of you to get poked.

### Question 23

Some people carry blood germs and feel totally fine, like a person who carries a cold but never sneezes — so we treat every drop of blood as if it might have germs.

### Question 24

You never eat, drink, or touch your eyes in the same place blood is handled — that would be like eating right next to a messy painting station and getting paint in your mouth.

### Question 25

If the sharps box is too full, you stop and get a fresh one — like taking out an overflowing trash bag instead of stomping it down.

### Question 26

If a needle falls, you use a grabber tool to pick it up, the way you would use tongs to grab something hot instead of your fingers.

### Question 27

Broken glass with blood on it is both sharp and germy, so you clean it up with a broom and dustpan, not your fingers.

### Question 28

Recapping is usually a no-no. In the rare case you must recap, you use a one-handed trick — scoop the cap up with the needle itself so your fingers stay out of the way.

### Question 29

If blood splashes in your eye, you rinse it with lots of water right away — like flushing out soap that got in your eye — and then tell your supervisor.

### Question 30

The safe order is like any accident: clean the spot, tell the grown-up in charge right away, then let the doctor or nurse check it out.

### Question 31

You tell someone right away after a poke so a doctor or nurse can step in fast — just like telling a coach about an injury so it can be treated before it gets worse.

### Question 32

The hepatitis B germ is tough — it can hang around on a counter for days, like a stubborn stain, so we have to clean surfaces really well.

### Question 33

OPIM is a list of special body fluids — like the fluid around the brain and joints — that we treat with the same care as blood, while sweat and plain tears are not on the list.

### Question 34

Plain spit is not on the 'special fluids' list unless you can see blood in it, but fluids like joint fluid and spinal fluid are always on the list.

### Question 35

You close the lid tight and carry the sharps box by its handle, standing straight up, so nothing can fall out along the way.

### Question 36

Cleaning up a blood spill is like cleaning a big juice spill but with a special germ-killing cleaner and gloves, so the spot is both wiped up and made safe.

### Question 37

Even clean-looking glass can cut you, and in a clinic a cut could let invisible germs in — so you use a broom and dustpan, not your hands.

### Question 38

A needleless system is the best kind of fix because it removes the sharp point altogether, like using a twist-off cap instead of a can opener.

### Question 39

An engineering control is like putting a cage around a dangerous machine so nobody can touch it, while PPE is like wearing gloves to touch the machine — the cage is safer.

### Question 40

A safety needle lowers the danger, like a car with airbags, but you still have to drive carefully and wear a seatbelt.

### Question 41

If you do not know how a new tool works, you ask before you use it — like reading the instructions before building a toy, not guessing halfway through.

### Question 42

The safety plan gets checked and refreshed every year — and any time the office starts doing something new — so the rules always match the real work.

### Question 43

Workers get safety training when they first start the job and then a refresher every year, like a yearly fire-drill refresher so everyone remembers what to do.

### Question 44

The office keeps a private notebook of needle pokes that lists what kind of needle and where it happened, so the office can spot patterns and fix the problem.

### Question 45

The results of a check-up after a needle poke are private, like a doctor's note — they stay locked up and are only shared if the worker says it is okay.

### Question 46

If a friend gets poked, you cheer them on to wash the spot and tell the boss right away, because hiding it could hurt their health.

### Question 47

A work-practice control is a smart setup habit, like putting the trash can right next to you before you start peeling vegetables so you never carry scraps across the room.

### Question 48

Putting the needle away right where you use it means you barely have to walk with it — fewer steps, fewer chances to trip or get poked.

### Question 49

The office offers the hepatitis B shot for free; if a worker says no thank you, they sign a paper saying they turned it down.

### Question 50

If you say no to the shot today but change your mind tomorrow, the office still has to give it to you for free.

### Question 51

If you see a teammate doing something dangerous, you kindly speak up and let the boss know — like telling a friend not to run with scissors.

### Question 52

Reusable sharp tools get carried in a strong, closed container — like putting dirty knives in a special carrying case instead of carrying them loose.

### Question 53

If your hands look dirty, use soap and water; if they look clean but you still touched patients, use the special hand gel.

### Question 54

Gloves are like disposable plates — you use a fresh one for each patient and throw it away, not reuse the same one all day.

### Question 55

If blood might squirt or splash, you put on a face shield like a goalie's mask to protect your eyes, nose, and mouth.

### Question 56

The best fix removes the danger itself; then come smart habits; and gloves and goggles are the last safety net — like a railing, careful walking, and finally a helmet.

### Question 57

If there is no sharps box nearby, you get a proper strong container before putting the needle away — you never use a flimsy cup or your pocket.

### Question 58

Every room where needles are used gets its own sharps box, so no one ever has to carry a used needle down the hall.

### Question 59

When the sharps box is full, you close it tight and it goes out with the special medical trash — you never dump it out and reuse the box.

### Question 60

The sharps box is only for pointy things that could poke someone — not for cotton balls, paper, or leftover drinks.

### Question 61

You cannot catch these blood germs just by hugging someone or sitting next to them — they need to get into your body through a poke or a splash.

### Question 62

The biohazard sign is like a 'beware' sticker that tells everyone the box holds germy, possibly sharp things.

### Question 63

The best way to avoid getting poked is to click the safety cover on the needle right away and drop it in the sharps box.

### Question 64

If you get poked at work, the office has to set up your check-up with a doctor or nurse and pay for it — like the workplace taking care of an on-the-job injury.

### Question 65

If you have a cut, you cover it with a bandage and wear gloves — like putting a patch on a hole in a raincoat before going out in the rain.

### Question 66

By writing down which needle caused a poke, the office can spot a problem product and switch to a safer one — like noticing a toy keeps breaking and buying a sturdier brand.

### Question 67

The assistant's job is to help set up safely and follow the rules, while the doctor or nurse is the one who does the procedure.

### Question 68

If a patient gets wiggly, the assistant helps keep them calm and lets the doctor or nurse take charge, rather than grabbing anything.

### Question 69

The counter gets wiped with germ-killing cleaner after every patient, like wiping the kitchen counter after every meal so germs do not hang around.

### Question 70

After gloves come off, you wash or gel your hands before you touch anything clean — like washing your hands after taking out the trash.

### Question 71

Your eyes, nose, and mouth are like open doors for germs, so you keep dirty hands away from your face.

### Question 72

Wash the poke with soap and water, do not squeeze it, tell your boss right away, and let the doctor or nurse check you — just like any injury, clean it and get help fast.

### Question 73

You should not squeeze a needle poke, because squeezing can bruise the spot and does not actually help — like pinching a splinter just makes it sore.

### Question 74

Clean-up is a careful job: gloves and goggles on, scoop the glass with a broom and dustpan, wipe with germ-killing cleaner, and throw everything away the safe way.

### Question 75

Gadgets that protect you automatically are engineering controls, smart habits are work-practice controls, and gear you wear is PPE.

### Question 76

If asked to do something you are not trained for, like giving a shot, the safe answer is to say no and get the doctor or nurse — even if you want to help.

### Question 77

The assistant helps with the paperwork and follows the rules, but the doctor or nurse is the one who orders the test and explains the results.

### Question 78

A safety system that leans only on gloves and hoping for the best is missing the stronger protections, like the sharps box and safety needles.

### Question 79

We treat every patient's blood the same careful way, no matter what we know about them — so an HIV diagnosis does not change the steps at all.

### Question 80

Some people hide a needle poke because they feel embarrassed, but hiding it means missing the help they need — so it is always better to speak up.

### Question 81

When the sharps box hits the fill line, you swap in a fresh box before adding more — you do not squish things down or jam more in.

### Question 82

Safety needles are helpful, like training wheels, but you still have to pedal carefully and wear a helmet.

### Question 83

Universal precautions started as 'be careful with blood,' and standard precautions grew into 'be careful with all body fluids, for every patient.'

### Question 84

If you have not learned how to clean a blood spill safely, you tell the boss and let someone trained handle it — like calling an adult for a big mess you are not sure how to clean.

### Question 85

Writing down each poke helps the office notice a pattern — like realizing one kind of ladder keeps causing falls — so it can buy safer equipment and teach better habits.

### Question 86

The workplace has to supply the whole safety package: a written plan, safety tools, free gloves and shields, the hepatitis B shot, training, and care after a poke.

### Question 87

Blood-safety training teaches you about how germs spread, how to wear gloves, and what to do after a poke — not how to argue about bills.

### Question 88

Blood liquid has special disposal rules — you follow the office's instructions for it, and you never pour it into the sharps box.

### Question 89

Keeping everyone safe is a team job that never stops — you follow the rules every day, speak up about problems, and keep learning.

### Question 90

To pick a safer needle, the office looks at its log of past pokes to see which brand kept causing trouble — like checking reviews before buying a new bike.
